insights.title: The archetype gives the plan; the champion decides the matchup
insights.principle: Knowing a champion's type tells you how its lane wants to be played. Whether that plan works against a particular opponent depends on the two champions' actual kits.
insights.why: Types are averages over very different kits. Between whole types the creator's ranked data sits close to even, while single champion pairs inside one type swing far wider, so a type label is a starting read, not a verdict.

example.text: Sona and Karma are both enchanters, yet Sona beats Karma about 60% of the time. Garen and Darius are both juggernauts; Garen is good into Jax and Darius is not.

insights.when: Use the type to decide what your lane is trying to do (trade, scale, all-in, poke). Use a champion-level matchup before you count a lane as won or lost.
insights.limits: The type averages and swings are one creator's Master+ figures on 26.21–26.22. A champion that sits between types (Sett, Aatrox, Zeri) inherits neither type's plan cleanly.
insights.siteNote: Draft Assistant already works at champion level: Counter labels come from per-champion DPM.LOL rows, never from a type. The Counter card's kit read says when the stored kits can't explain an edge.

claims.text: Type against type sits between 46% and 54%; inside one type a matchup can swing from 40% to 60%.
Sona beats Karma about 60% of the time.
Top lane class win rates barely differ; the champion decides.

insights.takeaway: Use the type to know the lane plan; check the champion pair before calling the lane won or lost.
insights.caveat: Type averages are one creator's Master+ figures.

matchups.text: Both enchanters, yet one wins the pair clearly: the type didn't decide it.
Two juggernauts into Jax: Garen's E still hits through Counter Strike, Darius's autos don't.
Darius leans on a Q Jax can step out of and autos Counter Strike dodges.

insights.title: Popularity and win rate are not the same as strength
insights.principle: A champion picked often can still lose more than it wins, and a hard champion's low win rate says as much about execution as about the champion.
insights.why: Pick rate follows comfort and reputation. Win rate across a whole ladder mixes the champion's power with how many players can execute it, so mechanically demanding champions look weaker in averages than in skilled hands.

example.text: Karma is among the most picked supports and wins about 48%. Ezreal, Lee Sin and Jayce are frequent picks with poor averages that the creator puts down to difficulty.

insights.when: Before treating a popular pick as safe, or a low win rate as a reason to avoid a champion someone on your team plays well.
insights.limits: A difficulty explanation is the creator's interpretation; the videos don't separate skill from strength in their numbers. Ranked averages are not pro priority, which Draft Assistant keeps apart.
insights.siteNote: Pro priority on Meta / Research keeps picks, bans, presence and win rate in separate columns and never reads presence as strength.

claims.text: Karma is the fourth most picked support at Master+ and wins about 48%.
Ezreal's, Lee Sin's and Jayce's low win rates reflect difficulty more than weakness.

insights.takeaway: Don't read pick rate as strength, or a hard champion's average as weakness.
insights.caveat: The difficulty explanation is the creator's reading, not separated in the data.

insights.title: Know a few champions' exact matchups rather than every class
insights.principle: Because single abilities decide matchups, a player is better served knowing one to three champions' specific good and bad matchups than knowing class trees for every champion.
insights.why: The class tree is too coarse to predict a lane. What actually transfers from game to game is knowing which enemy abilities beat your champion's kit, and that knowledge only builds on a small pool.

example.text: The top lane video closes on playing one to three top laners, so you know exactly which champions you're good against, bad against, and why.

insights.when: When building a role pool, and when deciding whether to blind a comfort pick or wait for a counter.
insights.limits: Advice for an individual player's pool. A team draft still needs flexibility across roles, which the videos don't discuss.

claims.text: Play one to three champions in a role and learn their exact matchups.

insights.takeaway: Learn one to three champions' exact matchups instead of every class tree.
insights.caveat: Advice for one player's pool, not for a team's flexibility.

insights.title: Six support types, each with one plan and one tool
insights.principle: Enchanters keep one carry alive, engage supports chain crowd control onto a target, wardens cancel the enemy's first move, hooks play around one long skillshot, mage supports win on range and damage, and misfits play a different lane altogether.
insights.why: Each type wins with one tool: a shield or heal, chained crowd control, a cancel, a hook, range control. The tree follows from those tools: engage, wardens and hooks beat enchanters; enchanters beat mages and misfits; anything that closes distance beats mages; wardens lose lane and win long games.

example.text: Leona's E roots and her Q stuns, about a second and a half of chained crowd control: a full combo at level 2 or 3 is usually a kill. Braum's shield instead decides how a fight ends by eating the enemy's projectiles.

insights.when: Before locking a support, name its type and ask what the enemy type does to it, then check whether your champion is one of the exceptions.
insights.limits: Exceptions are frequent: Nautilus loses to other engage supports, Braum loses to walk-in engage, Janna beats engage but loses to hooks, Yuumi beats mages but loses to hooks and engage. Type placement for hybrids (Karma, Seraphine, Neeko, Zilean) is the creator's choice.
insights.siteNote: The kit model stores how a champion starts fights (primary engage, catch, follow-up) and its peel and disengage, which cover the engage, hook and enchanter distinctions. It does not label support types.

claims.text: Type win rates: wardens 51.7%, engage 51.2%, hooks 51.2%, enchanters 50.1%, mage supports about 47–49%.
Wardens are about 290 gold behind at 15 minutes yet win 64% of long games; mage supports are about 280 gold ahead and win least.
The type tree and which champion belongs to which type.

insights.takeaway: Name your support's type, then check what the enemy type does to it and whether your champion is an exception.
insights.caveat: Exceptions are common: Nautilus, Braum, Janna and Yuumi all break the tree.

groups.label: Enchanters
groups.plan: Keep one carry alive; poke once per wave, save the shield or heal for their trade.
groups.vs: Beat mages and misfits; lose to engage and hooks.
groups.note: Karma is popular but last in win rate among enchanters.

groups.label: Engage
groups.plan: Hit level 2 first and chain crowd control onto the ADC.
groups.vs: Beat enchanters. Nautilus loses to the other engage supports.

groups.label: Wardens
groups.plan: Stand by the carry and cancel the enemy's first move.
groups.vs: Beat enchanters; lose lane, win long games. Braum loses to walk-in engage.

groups.label: Hooks
groups.plan: Play the lane around one long skillshot.
groups.vs: Beat enchanters and misfits; even against engage.

groups.label: Mage supports
groups.plan: Out-range and out-damage the lane; take plates.
groups.vs: Win lane, lose games: anything that closes distance beats them.

groups.label: Misfits
groups.plan: Each plays its own lane: a second carry, a roamer, an attached buffer.
groups.vs: Yuumi beats poke supports and loses to every hook and engage.

insights.title: Five ADC archetypes and the lane grid between them
insights.principle: Scalers want items and experience and win later; lane bullies want to fight as much as possible early; poke carries win trades from range; skirmishers fight on mobility; mage bot laners out-range everyone. Bullies beat skirmishers and scalers, poke beats scalers and skirmishers, and scalers win nothing in lane by design.
insights.why: Each archetype spends its strongest window differently. A bully that doesn't fight early wastes its window; a scaler that fights early spends health it needs to reach its items.

example.text: Kalista and Alistar into Ezreal and Bard are about 1,500 gold up at 15 minutes: a bully with an engage support doing exactly its job.

insights.when: Choosing a carry for the lane and the support you have, and deciding how hard to contest early trades.
insights.limits: Caitlyn is a bully who still scales. Skirmishers are champion-specific (Kai'Sa's engage, Xayah's feathers). Mage bot strength is a 26.21 meta observation.
insights.siteNote: Each kit stores a power curve (early, mid, late) and lane pressure, which is how the site already tells a bully from a scaler.

claims.text: The archetype lane grid.
Kalista + Alistar about 1,500 gold up at 15 minutes in the example game.

insights.takeaway: Know what your ADC's archetype wants from the lane before you pick the duo or decide how hard to trade.
insights.caveat: The grid is lane tendency, not a game result; single champions break it often.

groups.label: Scalers
groups.plan: Lose lane as little as possible, reach items, win later fights.
groups.vs: Win nothing in lane, even into skirmishers. A hyper scaler can be outscaled by another (Twitch over Jinx).

groups.label: Lane bullies
groups.plan: Fight as much as possible early and turn the lead into objectives.
groups.vs: Beat scalers and skirmishers in lane; can't stick to poke.
groups.note: Caitlyn is a bully on range who still scales.

groups.label: Poke / casters
groups.plan: Win trades from range until the enemy can't stand in lane.
groups.vs: Harass scalers and skirmishers; can die to bullies when greedy. Winning trades doesn't win all-ins.
groups.note: Jhin and Ashe are utility casters; Varus depends on his build.

groups.label: Skirmishers
groups.plan: Fight on mobility in each champion's own window.
groups.vs: Take time to scale; weaker into poke and bullies.
groups.note: Zeri is technically a caster: her Q is her auto attack.

groups.label: Mage bots
groups.plan: Out-range everyone, clear waves, peak in the mid game.
groups.vs: Win lane against every archetype in the creator's 26.21 data; immobile once reached. Short-range mages like Cassiopeia don't fit.

matchups.text: A bully with an engage support doing its job against a poke duo: the lane is decided early.

stat.text: About 1,500 gold up at 15 in the example game

insights.title: Top lane classes: purpose and weakness
insights.principle: Juggernauts want long trades up close and struggle to get there; divers burst in and out and suffer when their engage is denied; skirmishers duel in short bursts and struggle against what they can't auto-attack; tanks trade on cooldowns and fear kiting and percent-health damage; ranged top laners abuse range and fear hard engage.
insights.why: Each class's weakness is the thing its win pattern depends on. That gives the tree: juggernauts beat tanks, divers jump ranged champions, skirmishers beat tanks, tanks beat divers and ranged champions, and ranged champions kite juggernauts.

example.text: Renekton dives in, trades, and tries to E out; Darius pulls him back and wins the extended fight. A diver who can get further out avoids the pull.

insights.when: As the first question about a top matchup: which part of my class's pattern can this opponent deny?
insights.limits: The creator says himself that class win rates barely differ in top lane and that specific abilities overturn the tree often. Treat the tree as a vocabulary, not a prediction.

claims.text: Class labels are Riot's; the tree between them is the creator's.

insights.takeaway: Ask which part of your class's pattern the opponent can deny.
insights.caveat: Class win rates barely differ in top lane; use the tree as vocabulary, not prediction.

groups.label: Juggernauts
groups.plan: Long trades up close.
groups.vs: Beat tanks; get kited by ranged top laners.
groups.note: Sett sits between juggernaut and bruiser.

groups.label: Divers / bruisers
groups.plan: Burst in, trade, get out.
groups.vs: Jump ranged top laners; lose to tanks.

groups.label: Skirmishers
groups.plan: Short bursts and strong duels.
groups.vs: Strong into tanks; struggle against what they can't auto-attack.

groups.label: Tanks
groups.plan: Trade on cooldowns and win by being hard to kill.
groups.vs: Beat divers and ranged; weak to kiting, %HP damage and hyper scalers.

groups.label: Ranged
groups.plan: Abuse range with autos and abilities.
groups.vs: Kite juggernauts; fear hard engage.
groups.note: Gangplank is a hybrid with barrels and Q.

matchups.text: Renekton trades well, but Darius pulls him back as he dashes out and wins the extended fight.

insights.title: Jungle archetypes share one loop and differ in their goal
insights.principle: Tempo gankers, power farmers, skirmishers, tanks and assassins all farm and gank only when the gank is close to guaranteed. They differ in what they do with a lead and in when they need it.
insights.why: A tempo ganker converts ganks more reliably, a farmer converts gold into a later spike, a skirmisher wins river 2v2s and 3v3s, a tank gets value from crowd control and ultimates whatever its gold, and an assassin snowballs off one target. Forcing ganks a champion can't convert costs the camps it needed.

example.text: Master Yi power farms and only takes dragon when he knows Lee Sin is far away, but takes tower dives when his Q makes them safe. Hecarim forces river fights into a Qiyana because he wins the early skirmishes.

insights.when: Choosing a jungler for the lanes you have, and judging whether the enemy jungler's early pressure is a real threat to your plan.
insights.limits: The jungle matchup itself matters least, because junglers can avoid each other; a bad jungle matchup can still be a good team matchup. Archetype placements (Elise tempo, Cho'Gath leaning farmer, Nunu leaning tempo) are the creator's.
insights.siteNote: The Jungle tab shows which junglers pros paired with which mids and what was on the enemy board at the pick; the kit curve separates early tempo junglers from farmers.

claims.text: Hecarim beats Qiyana 57% (1,252 games).
The jungler's win rate depends most on their own gold lead of any role.
Jungle matchups are the least important of the five lanes.

insights.takeaway: Every jungler farms and ganks only when it's guaranteed; pick by what it does with a lead.
insights.caveat: The jungle matchup itself matters least: junglers can avoid each other.

groups.label: Tempo gankers
groups.plan: Reach gankable lanes first and snowball the team.
groups.vs: Out-pace farmers and tanks; the right one beats skirmishers in 2v2s.
groups.note: Nunu leans tempo because his ganks are so strong.

groups.label: Power farmers
groups.plan: Farm to a 2–3 item spike; gank only what's guaranteed.
groups.vs: Lose early to almost everyone except tanks.
groups.note: Cho'Gath leans farmer: he stacks his ultimate first.

groups.label: Skirmishers
groups.plan: Win river 2v2s and 3v3s.
groups.vs: Strong against almost everyone early.

groups.label: Tanks
groups.plan: Start fights; stay useful far behind on gold.
groups.vs: Lose most matchups but don't need to worry about assassins.

groups.label: Assassins
groups.plan: Pick one target and snowball off them.
groups.vs: Punish farmers; can't take the long fights tanks and skirmishers want.

matchups.text: A skirmisher forces early fights an assassin can't take yet.
Once ahead, an assassin invades the moment the other is seen: assassin against assassin depends on who has the lead.

insights.title: Ask whether your abilities work against theirs
insights.principle: Before trusting a matchup, check whether the opponent has one ability that switches off the thing your champion wins with.
insights.why: Several top and support matchups hinge on a single interaction. Jax's E dodges basic attacks but not abilities, so ability-based juggernauts keep their damage while auto-attack juggernauts lose theirs. Shen's W blocks basic attacks, which removes an auto-weaving champion's trades.

example.text: Garen's E keeps hitting Jax through Counter Strike and his ultimate finishes the trade; Darius and Sett lose much of their damage while it is up. Irelia can barely auto Malphite or Shen in a trade.

insights.when: Picking into a revealed lane opponent, and reading a counter label: does the edge come from an ability interaction?
insights.limits: Interactions decide individual trades, not whole lanes: wave state, jungle help and items still move the result. The win rates attached are the creator's ranked figures.

tools.label: Counter card in the Draft Room

insights.siteNote: The Counter card's kit read compares stored kit values only and says so: cooldowns and ability interactions like these are not stored, so it can't explain an edge that rests on them.

claims.text: Jax's Counter Strike dodges basic attacks; abilities still hit him.
Shen's Spirit's Refuge blocks basic attacks.
Three ability-based juggernauts win 54–56% into Jax; Darius and Sett win 47%.

insights.takeaway: Before trusting a lane, check for one enemy ability that switches off what your champion wins with.
insights.caveat: Interactions decide trades, not whole lanes.

matchups.text: Counter Strike dodges autos, not abilities: Garen's E keeps hitting.
Shen's W blocks the autos Ambessa weaves between abilities, and his E forces the trade when she's out of them.
Malphite's E cuts Irelia's attack speed; she can barely auto him.

insights.title: Melee into ranged: can you actually close the gap?
insights.principle: A melee champion only beats a ranged one if its kit reliably reaches the target; a ranged champion only escapes if it has the tool to answer that reach.
insights.why: A ranged laner wins by trading from where the melee can't answer. A hard gap-closer (Nasus's W slowing the target, Irelia dashing through minions, Pantheon's jump) removes that space; without one the melee champion pays health to walk in and gets kited.

example.text: Darius has to Flash to reach Vayne and still gets kited out; Nasus's W slows Jayce enough that Nasus wins about 57%. Irelia beats Jayce but Yone, also a skirmisher, gets pushed off by hammer E.

insights.when: Picking a melee laner into a ranged one, or a ranged laner into a melee one: name the gap-closer and the answer (Kennen's E speed, Gangplank's W cleanse, Jayce's knockback).
insights.limits: Ranged laners that win lane still need to convert the lead, and late-game value can reverse the matchup (see the conversion lesson).

tools.label: Counter card in the Draft Room

insights.siteNote: Stored kits keep range and self-peel (the site's proxy for mobility) and reach to a protected target; the Counter card names range and mobility differences when they are one-sided.

claims.text: Gangplank's W cleanses crowd control.
Nasus beats Jayce about 57%.

insights.takeaway: Melee into ranged only works if your kit reliably reaches the target; name the gap-closer and their answer.

matchups.text: Wither slows Jayce enough that he can't kite.
Darius has to Flash to reach Vayne and still gets kited.
Irelia dashes through minions to reach Jayce.
Yone runs at Jayce with E and gets pushed off by hammer E.

insights.title: Projectile blockers lose to engage that walks in
insights.principle: Tools that stop projectiles beat hook engage and do nothing against supports who walk or dash in; and a hook engage is helpless while its hook is on cooldown.
insights.why: Braum's shield eats Nautilus's hook, so Braum wins that lane. Rell, Leona and Alistar don't throw anything: they run at you, so the shield has nothing to block. Nautilus's hook also stops on the first unit hit, which lets other engage supports close the distance while it is down.

example.text: Alistar walks in while Nautilus's hook is on cooldown and Nautilus has nothing left to answer with. Braum puts his wall between Blitzcrank and his ADC and the hook never lands.

insights.when: Picking a support into a revealed engage or hook support, or choosing between a warden and an enchanter against them.
insights.limits: Individual matchups, Master+ ranked; Braum's overall strength in the data (half of all warden games) inflates the warden average.
insights.siteNote: Not modelled: the kit model stores how a champion starts a fight, not whether the start is a projectile, so the Counter card can't use this to explain an edge.

claims.text: Braum's Unbreakable blocks projectiles, not dashes.
Nautilus's Q stops on the first unit hit.
Braum beats Nautilus 56% and loses to Rell, Leona and Alistar.

insights.takeaway: Projectile blockers stop hooks, not engage that walks or dashes in.
insights.caveat: Braum is half of all warden games in the data.

matchups.text: Braum's shield eats the hook.
Rell throws nothing for the shield to block; Leona and Alistar beat Braum the same way.
Alistar walks in while the hook is on cooldown.

insights.title: Disengage is a cooldown, not a counter
insights.principle: A disengage tool cancels one engage. It wins the lane only if it is held for that engage, and while it is on cooldown the engage support has the window.
insights.why: Disengage supports as a group go even against engage supports. Each tool also has gaps: Braum's shield doesn't stop a dash, Milio's ultimate doesn't remove knock-ups, Morgana's Black Shield doesn't block physical damage, and Janna's knock-up needs time that a hook doesn't give.

example.text: Nautilus hooks in and Poppy's W stops him mid-dash, so the all-in never happens. Janna beats Alistar, Leona and Rakan but loses to Thresh.

insights.when: Choosing a peel or disengage support into engage: check which engage tool it actually stops, and plan to hold it rather than spend it on poke.
insights.limits: A lane habit as much as a draft rule. In team fights several engage tools arrive at once and one cancel covers only one of them.

tools.label: Comp Check in the Draft Room

insights.siteNote: Comp Check already counts disengage and counter-engage as separate kit facts and reads a missing anti-engage plan as a weakness.

claims.text: Poppy's Steadfast Presence stops dashes around her.
Milio's ultimate does not remove knock-ups.
Morgana's Black Shield blocks magic damage and crowd control, not physical damage.
Disengage supports together win 50% against engage supports.

insights.takeaway: Hold the disengage for the engage; while it's down, step back.
insights.caveat: In a team fight several engage tools arrive at once.

matchups.text: Poppy's W stops Nautilus mid-dash, so the all-in never happens.
Janna's knock-up needs time to charge; a hook doesn't wait.

insights.title: Immobile mages lose to anything that reaches them
insights.principle: A long-range mage wins the lane on range, but once something reaches it there is no dash or shield to save it.
insights.why: Mage supports have the best lane of any support type and the lowest win rate; engage beats them about 61% of the time. In bot lane, mage carries out-range even Caitlyn, and the counterplay is the same: most of them can't move away.

example.text: Pyke's ultimate executes a squishy mage support like Lux; a tank never drops low enough. Ziggs and Xerath clear and poke from far beyond Caitlyn, but are immobile once reached.

insights.when: Facing a mage support or mage bot laner: pick a champion that closes distance. Picking a mage: check whether the enemy can reach you.
insights.limits: Range only wins while the mage can keep it; Cassiopeia's short range is why she doesn't fit bot lane. Mage bot strength is a 26.21 meta observation and may not last.

tools.label: Counter card in the Draft Room

claims.text: Mage supports win about 47–49%; engage supports beat them about 61%.
Mage bot laners: Karthus about 58–60%, Vel'Koz, Aurelion Sol, Hwei and Syndra 54% or more.
Mage bots peak in the mid game, so the game is often decided before the ADC outscales.

insights.takeaway: Facing a long-range mage, pick something that reaches it; picking one, check what can reach you.
insights.caveat: Mage bot strength is a 26.21 observation.

matchups.text: Pyke's execute finds a squishy mage support; a tank never drops low enough.

insights.title: Off-role lane winners: refuse the first all-in
insights.principle: Off-role supports like Pantheon, Camille and Zoe are built to win the first all-in. Against them, don't take the level 2 fight and the game turns in your favour once laning ends.
insights.why: Their lead comes from one early window; outside lane most of them win 48% or less. Denying that window removes their plan.

example.text: Camille and Zoe supports average over 500 gold up at 15 minutes, yet Pantheon, Camille and Sylas win 48% or less. Only Elise is above 50%.

insights.when: Facing an off-role support in bot lane: play behind minions and give up the first trade.
insights.limits: Only applies when the enemy pick is a genuine lane-only plan; Elise and some others carry value later.

claims.text: Camille +525 and Zoe +532 gold at 15; Pantheon +362.

insights.takeaway: Against an off-role support, give up the level 2 fight and win after lane.

insights.title: Match the support to what the ADC wants
insights.principle: A bot lane works when both champions want the same thing: a bully wants a support who starts fights early, a scaler wants one who keeps it alive until its items, and a poke carry wants room to trade from range.
insights.why: An early bully paired with a support who can't start a fight has nothing to convert its damage into; a scaler paired with an all-in support is dragged into fights before it is ready. The duo's ADC type matters more than the support's type.

example.text: Ezreal + Nautilus wins about 42%: two different goals. Lane bully + mage support wins about 43%. Wardens with a scaling ADC win about 57%, Braum + Yunara 57.1%, Rakan + Xayah 55.1%.

insights.when: Picking the second half of a bot lane. With a Leona, lock a Samira or Draven; with a Lulu, a Xayah or someone who scales.
insights.limits: Pairings have their own exceptions (Lulu with Kog'Maw, Twitch or Yunara; Janna with Aphelios). The averages favour engage over enchanters partly because enchanters have a lower base win rate, as the ADC video itself notes. Pro bot lanes often pair a bully with a support who doesn't start fights: Lucian + Milio and Kalista + Renata Glasc are among the most recorded pairs in this site's 2026 pro games, so read this as a solo-queue lane heuristic, not a rule.

tools.label: Comp Check in the Draft Room

insights.siteNote: Comp Check reads the bot duo's engage and follow-up ("Support engages, carry cannot follow", "Short-range carry without a protector"). It does not warn about a bully without an engage support, because recorded pro play contradicts that as a rule.
insights.disagreement: The support video says Lulu with hyper scalers has a huge win rate and Aphelios + Lulu only 44%; the ADC video says hyper scalers do better with engage supports who also peel, then concedes the engage edge mostly reflects enchanters' lower base win rate. The series never controls for that base rate, so neither reading is established.

claims.text: Ezreal + Nautilus about 42%; mage support + lane bully about 43%; wardens + scaling ADC about 57%.
Lane bullies want engage supports.

insights.takeaway: Pick the support for what your ADC wants: early fights, protection until items, or room to trade.
insights.caveat: A solo-queue heuristic: pro bully lanes often pair with supports who don't start fights.

matchups.text: Two goals: an all-in support with a carry who wants to trade from range.
A warden keeps a scaling carry alive until she carries.
Engage that dashes back to the carry it fights beside.

insights.title: A lane lead wins nothing until it is converted
insights.principle: Lane bullies, ranged top laners and tempo junglers win by turning an early lead into objectives and pressure; the gold alone does not win the game.
insights.why: Early champions trade late-game value for an early window. If the lead isn't pushed into towers, dragons and map pressure while the window is open, the scaling side catches up and the lead stops mattering.

example.text: A Grandmaster Draven is 3,500 gold up at 15 minutes and still loses the Baron fight and the game. Jayce beats Malphite in lane, but one gank resets him, and Shen out-impacts a Jayce 1,400 gold ahead once fights start.

insights.when: Drafting an early-game pick: make sure the rest of the comp can take objectives with that lead (lane priority, a jungler who follows, a way to start fights).
insights.limits: Some bullies scale fine (Caitlyn). Lane bullies with a real lead (300+ gold at 15) win 63% in the creator's data, so the lesson is about conversion, not about avoiding bullies.
insights.siteNote: Comp Check's timing read and the tempo plan already ask whether an early comp has a way to use its window; lane priority for sieges is a separate check.

claims.text: Lane bullies with a 300+ gold lead at 15 minutes win 63%.
The lead isn't what wins the game, it's the conversion.

insights.takeaway: An early pick needs a comp that can turn its lead into objectives.
insights.caveat: Bullies with a real lead still win 63% in the creator's data.

matchups.text: Jayce wins the lane, but one gank resets him: a ranged top who isn't ahead is behind.

insights.title: Scalers, tanks and wardens are judged by the late game
insights.principle: Some picks are meant to lose lane: their job is to lose as little as possible and arrive at the late game, where they decide fights.
insights.why: Scalers win once their items arrive; tanks and wardens get their value from crowd control, ultimates and protection rather than gold, so they matter even from behind. Judging them by lane gold misreads the plan.

example.text: Jinx is almost always behind after laning and still matches lane bullies' win rate. Kayle loses lane to K'Sante and dominates later. A Nunu 3,000 gold down still out-impacts the enemy jungler.

insights.when: Drafting a scaling carry or a tank: protect the lane rather than contest it, and make sure the comp can survive until its spike.
insights.limits: Tanks fall behind hyper scalers who are as strong as them early and outscale them later. A comp of only late picks still has to survive the early game.
insights.siteNote: Stored power curves and resource demand already separate scalers and low-economy tanks; Comp Check names a scaling plan and its timing.

claims.text: Tank junglers have the highest win rate of any archetype when behind.
Wardens win 46% of short games, 56% of medium and 64% of long ones.
Tanks never really win lane, and never really lose it.

insights.takeaway: Judge a scaler or tank by the fight it arrives at, not by lane gold.

matchups.text: K'Sante wins the early lane; Kayle outscales and kills him through his ultimate.
Jayce is 1,400 gold up after lane; Shen still forces the fights that matter.

insights.title: A tempo lead has a deadline
insights.principle: A comp built on early tempo must end the game, or at least break the map open, before the enemy's scaling and tank value arrive.
insights.why: Tempo junglers and early carries are strongest in the first half of the game; tanks and hyper carries keep gaining value. A lead that is still a lead at Elder is often already lost.

example.text: Lee Sin is about 2,000 gold up at 15 minutes and takes soul and two Barons, then loses the Elder fight to Zac and the enemy hyper carries.

insights.when: Choosing between an early jungler and a scaling one: does the rest of the comp help end the game early, or does it want time?
insights.limits: One illustrative game. Whether a team 'should have ended' is the creator's interpretation.

claims.text: Lee Sin did nothing wrong; his team didn't end the game in time.

insights.takeaway: An early tempo comp has to end, or break the map, before scaling arrives.

matchups.text: Lee Sin's 2,000 gold lead, soul and two Barons, then the Elder fight goes to Zac and the enemy hyper carries.
